passage: Sumit, you asked why I still call my mother every Sunday, though she once made me feel like a traitor for leaving. Sit; I will tell you. At twenty-four I got an offer from a firm two cities away. My mother stopped speaking to me for nine days, and I lay awake feeling like a traitor. Then came the headaches every time I mentioned it, and the line, "Go, go, if it finishes me, so be it." I nearly turned the offer down. What changed was a cousin saying, "Love could have said I will miss you." So I told my mother, gently, that I was going, that I would call every Sunday and come home for every festival. She sulked for a month, then began posting me pickles. The guilt lasted longer than the sulk. Mridul

qa.q: How many days did Mridul's mother stop speaking after the offer?
qa.a: She stopped speaking to Mridul for nine days.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling during the nine days of silence?
qa.a: Mridul felt guilty and torn, lying awake feeling like a traitor.

qa.q: How did Mridul set a boundary while keeping warmth?
qa.a: Mridul said gently that the move was happening and promised to call every Sunday and come home for every festival.

qa.q: How might the mother have seen the move?
qa.a: Her silence and talk of being finished suggest she feared being left alone, though it was not a fair way to say so.

grounding: An elder recalls a parent controlling through silence, headaches and guilt, and how gentle firm boundaries and warmth carried through.

passage:
"Mummy, the hostel is only forty minutes away. I'll come home every Sunday."

Indu pressed a hand to her chest. "Go, then. My BP is already high. If something happens to me at night, who will know?"

"Mummy, you have Papa, and Mrs. Joshi next door."

"Papa doesn't notice anything. You're my only daughter." A long silence. Then: "I suppose I didn't raise you right."

Deepika's throat tightened. The old guilt rose, the one that always ended with her unpacking her bag.

"Mummy, I love you. It's not about you. The night shifts at the hospital end at two. I can't travel home safely at that hour."

"So I'm the problem."

"No. You're my mother, and I'm going. I'll call every night at nine, and I'll be here Sunday for lunch."

Indu turned away. Deepika hugged her anyway. That evening she called Sheela masi, who said, "You did right, beta. I'll check on your mother."

qa.q: How far away is the hostel?
qa.a: The hostel is only forty minutes away.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel when her mother said she hadn't raised her right?
qa.a: Deepika felt the old guilt tightening her throat, the kind that usually made her give in.

qa.q: How did Deepika set a boundary while keeping warmth?
qa.a: She explained her reason, stayed firm about moving, offered nightly calls and Sunday lunches, hugged her mother, and sought support from Sheela masi.

qa.q: How does Indu see Deepika's move?
qa.a: Indu sees it as abandonment, using her health and guilt to try to keep Deepika home.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young woman whose mother uses guilt and illness to control her choices, who sets a gentle, firm boundary, keeps warmth and seeks support.

passage:
I'm Jahnavi, and until last year, my mother Aparna's silence ran my life.

Whenever I made a choice she didn't like, Amma just stopped speaking. When I chose commerce instead of medicine, eleven days. When I cut my hair short, four days. When I said I wanted to take the job in Hyderabad, she didn't speak to me for three weeks, and I felt like the worst daughter alive.

I kept apologising for wanting things.

My friend's aunt, who is a counsellor, said something that changed how I saw it: "Silence used to punish isn't love. And it isn't your fault."

So when the Hyderabad offer came again, I didn't wait for Amma's permission. I told her gently, "Amma, I'm taking it. I'll call you every Sunday." She went silent. I kept calling every Sunday anyway, talking even when she didn't answer.

In the seventh week, she said, "Are you eating properly?" It was a start. I also began seeing a counsellor myself.

qa.q: How many days did Amma stop speaking when Jahnavi cut her hair short?
qa.a: She stopped speaking for four days.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel during Amma's three weeks of silence?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt guilty, like the worst daughter alive, and kept apologising for wanting things.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi set a gentle, firm boundary?
qa.a: She told Amma kindly she was taking the job, kept calling every Sunday regardless of the silence, and sought support from a counsellor.

qa.q: How might Aparna experience the Sunday calls?
qa.a: She may feel hurt and resistant at first, but slowly softens, as her question about eating properly shows.

grounding: A first-person account shows a young woman whose mother controls her with silence, who recognises it is not love or her fault, sets a gentle firm boundary, keeps warmth and seeks support.
